name: Exponential Metric of Papapetrou and Yilmaz
description: A static, spherically symmetric metric whose components are exponentials of the Newtonian potential, with no horizon, offered in place of Schwarzschild's and later shown to be a traversable wormhole held open by a scalar field of negative energy.
convention: The mass enters as the length $m = GM/c^2$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The exponential metric has no horizon [boonserm2018]. Its line element is $ds^2 = -e^{-2m/r}c^2dt^2 + e^{2m/r}\left(dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2\right)$ with $m = GM/c^2$, and $e^{-2m/r}$ is positive at every $r > 0$, so $g_{tt}$ never vanishes [boonserm2018]. Far from the mass it reads $g_{ab} = \eta_{ab} + (2m/r)\delta_{ab}$, which "exactly matches the lowest-order weak-field expansion of general relativity", so it passes the weak field tests that Schwarzschild's metric passes [boonserm2018]. Achilles Papapetrou wrote it down first, in 1954, while studying metrics whose components depend on the coordinates through one scalar field alone [papapetrou1954, makukov2018]. Huseyin Yilmaz, at the Sylvania laboratories in Waltham, Massachusetts, found it again four years later [yilmaz1958, makukov2018].¶Yilmaz's paper offered "a generally covariant scalar field theory of gravitation" that "predicts correctly the results of the three crucial tests of general relativity" [yilmaz1958]. In a footnote he noted that the metric solves Einstein's equations with the stress of a massless scalar field entered with its sign reversed [makukov2018]. By 1992 his theory put a stress tensor of the gravitational field itself on the right hand side of Einstein's equations, beside that of matter, and its static fields were $ds^2 = -e^{2\Phi}d(ct)^2 + e^{-2\Phi}\left(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2\right)$, the exponential metric in Cartesian coordinates when $\Phi = -m/r$ [misner1999].¶Could a theory of gravity with no black holes in it be right? In December 1994 the question made the news, under the headline "Theorists Make a Bid to Eliminate Black Holes" [misner1999]. Charles Misner, at the University of Maryland, answered in April 1995 with a paper called "Yilmaz Cancels Newton" [misner1999]. He argued that the added stress changes the equations of motion of a fluid so as "to remove all gravitational forces" in the Newtonian limit, which allows "a solar system in which the Sun and the planets are permanently at rest" [misner1999]. Carroll Alley and Per Kennett Aschan, of the same department, replied with Yilmaz two months later that Misner's claim "is based on a false premise" [alley1995].¶Among the X-ray binaries the black hole candidates might be heavy neutron stars with surfaces, and in 1998 Stanley Robertson used the metric, without the theory, to test the idea [robertson1998]. He found an innermost marginally stable orbit whose "radius, binding energy and Keplerian frequency" are "within a few percent of the same quantities for the Schwarzschild metric" [robertson1998]. The metric also turned up, under no name, in Kirill Bronnikov's catalogue of the static spheres that a massless scalar field of negative energy can support, where it is "Branch B", the case $k = 0$, and the field grows in proportion to $1/r$, a harmonic coordinate [bronnikov2011]. With J. C. Fabris and A. Zhidenko he recorded in 2011 that its spheres have a smallest member, a throat that "has the size $e \cdot m$" [bronnikov2011]. Its far end, $r \to 0$, is in their words "a singular horizon": the curvature goes to zero there, and still the metric's behaviour "makes its continuation impossible" [bronnikov2011].¶What lies on the other side of $r = m$? Petarpa Boonserm, Tritos Ngampitipan, Alex Simpson, and Matt Visser put the question to the metric in 2018 [boonserm2018]. The sphere at $r$ has area $4\pi r^2e^{2m/r}$, which is least at $r = m$ and grows again inside it, so Schwarzschild's horizon at $r = m/2$ in isotropic coordinates is replaced here by "a traversable wormhole throat" in the sense of Michael Morris and Kip Thorne [boonserm2018, morris1988]. Beyond the throat is an "infinite-volume 'other universe'" where "time runs slower", and in the areal radius $R = re^{m/r}$, which turns back at the throat, the metric needs Lambert's function, $r = -m/\mathrm{W}(-m/R)$ [boonserm2018]. On the near side light circles at $r = 2m$ and matter orbits stably down to $r = (3 + \sqrt{5})m$, each "not too far" from Schwarzschild's value [boonserm2018]. The throat is held open by a scalar field of negative kinetic energy, $R_{ab} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\nabla_a\Phi\nabla_b\Phi$ with $\Phi = 2m/r$, so that, "perhaps ironically", a metric championed by people who reject general relativity solves Einstein's equations [boonserm2018].

related.text: The metric it was offered in place of. The two agree at first order in $m/r$, and Schwarzschild's horizon at $r = m/2$ in isotropic coordinates is replaced by a throat at $r = m$ [boonserm2018].

The same matter, a massless scalar field of negative energy, with the mass set to zero where the exponential metric has Bronnikov's constant $k$ set to zero. Both belong to the anti-Fisher family, and both have a throat [bronnikov2011].

The same field with its energy positive, around a naked singularity. The exponential metric is its limit $\gamma \to \infty$ with $\gamma b = 2m$ held fixed, $(1 - 2m/\gamma r)^\gamma \to e^{-2m/r}$, which takes the field's energy negative [makukov2018].
The general traversable wormhole. The exponential metric is one, with a throat of areal radius $e\,m$ and clocks beyond the throat running slow [boonserm2018].

The weak field with a number in front of every term. Expanded in $m/r$, the exponential metric has $\beta = \gamma = 1$, the values of general relativity, so the classical tests cannot tell it from Schwarzschild's [yilmaz1958, boonserm2018].

coordinates.name: Isotropic
coordinates.convention: We use isotropic coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so a dot on $t$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Cartesian
coordinates.convention: We use the Cartesian coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$ of the isotropic chart, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the isotropic radius, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so a dot on $t$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Areal (curvature coordinates)

parameters.description: Isotropic radius, a length, the solution of $re^{m/r} = R$ on the chart's side of the throat, with $\mathrm{W}$ Lambert's function, $\mathrm{W}(x)\,e^{\mathrm{W}(x)} = x$; its derivative is $\partial_R r = r^2/\left(R\left(r - m\right)\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, R, \theta, \phi)$ with $R = re^{m/r}$ the areal radius, $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and $r$ the isotropic radius, a function of $R$. The chart covers one side of the throat $R = em$: $\mathrm{W}$ is the principal branch of Lambert's function where $r > m$ and its branch $\mathrm{W}_{-1}$ where $r < m$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so a dot on $t$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Harmonic
coordinates.convention: We use Bronnikov's harmonic coordinate $u = 1/r$, an inverse length, with $r$ the isotropic radius and $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so a dot on $t$ in the geodesic equations means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{u} - m\,u^4e^{-4m\,u}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{2 - m\,u}{u}\dot{u}^2 + u\left(1 - m\,u\right)\dot{\theta}^2 + u\left(1 - m\,u\right)\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
